To work through questions of distribution, we'll use the dataset from Bertrand & Mullainathan's 2004 study, "Are Emily and Greg More Employable Than Lakisha and Jamal? A Field Experiment on Labor Market Discrimination". In this study, the authors sent out 4870 fake resumes, which they had randomly assigned to have either an African-American or White sounding name. They found that White names receive 50 percent more callbacks for interviews. 
The dataset, which you can download locally [here](https://www.openintro.org/data/csv/labor_market_discrimination.csv), lists every resume and the job it was sent to. 

```{webr}
#| context: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/emzou/r-guide/main/r-code/visuals/labor_market_discrimination.csv",
  "labor.csv"
)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{webr}
df <- read_csv("labor.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

# Histograms
The `years_exp` column in our dataframe indicates how many years of experience were listed on the fake resume. 
We're interested in how diverse the resumes in the dataset are in terms of years of experience.  We can use a histogram to visualize this. 
A histogram shows the distribution of a single quantitative variable by splitting the observations into equal-width intervals (bins), and then counting how many observations fall into each one.

Similar to other ggplot2 functions, all we need to make a histogram is the geom_histogram() function, and to specify our variable of interest in the aes() call. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
ggplot(df, aes(years_exp)) +
  geom_histogram()
```

As always, we want our visuals to be easy to read. 
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
ggplot(df, aes(years_exp)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "#4C72B0", color = "white", boundary = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "Years of work experience listed on resume",
    x = "Years of experience",
    y = "Number of resumes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )      
```

### binwidth 
Notice that in geom_histogram(), we also set the `binwidth` to 2. This means that the each bar counts up the total count of every two years -- 0-2, 2-4, and so on. Try changing binwidth in the above code and see what happpens. 

## Interpretation 
Looking at the visual, we can see that the resumes are not uniformly distributed across years of experience, and that resumes generally have less years of experience. 


# How are histograms different from bar plots? 

The histogram looks exactly the same as a bar plot, so why do we differentiate them? 
Put another way, why do we require that only interval variables can be depicted with histograms, rather than nominal and ordinal ones? 

## Occupation 
To think through this, we'll make a bar plot for the `occup_broad` column, which categorizes the jobs a resume applied to into Executive, Administrative, Sales representatives, Sales workers, Secretaries, and Clerical. 
This makes it a **nominal** variable. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
df |>
  mutate(
    occup_broad = factor(
      occup_broad,
      levels = 1:6,
      labels = c("Executives &\nmanagerial", "Administrative\nsupervisors",
                 "Sales\nrepresentatives", "Sales\nworkers",
                 "Secretaries &\nlegal assistants", "Clerical")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = occup_broad)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#4C72B0", width = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Broad occupation category of the job ad",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of resumes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10)
  )
```

Compare this plot to the years of experience plot. In a histogram, the overall shape of the data tells us what the distribution of the data is, we can learn something about the data when our eyes move across the x-axis. In a bar plot of a nominal variable, the order of the x-axis doesn't matter. You can rearrange the categories however you want and you'll still have the same information. In the histogram, we can see that as years of experience increases, the less resumes there are. 

## Education
`education` lists the highest level of education reported on each resume, which ranges from: 1 = high school dropout; 2 = high school graduate; 3 = some college; 4 = College graduate or more, (and 0 for not reported). This makes it an **ordinal** variable, because the order of the categories matter. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
df |>
  filter(education != 0) |>
  mutate(
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = 1:4,
      labels = c("HS dropout", "HS graduate",
                 "Some college", "College graduate or more")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#4C72B0", width = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Education level listed on resume",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of resumes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10)
  )
```

At first glance, this seems to function very similarly as the years of experience histogram -- we can see that (whatever distribution pattern)

However, the intervals on the x-axis are not equal. From the perspective of someone reading the resume, we can imagine that there is some difference in  the evaluation of high school dropout applicants and high school graduate applicants. But is this difference the same as how someone with some college is compared to someone with a high school graduate? 

More importantly, you can tell very different stories with the same data based on how you create categories, or even just choosing  bin width. 

# How to lie with real data

The `frac_black` column indicates the proportion of Black residents in each (fictional) applicant's zipcode. 
Below, we make a histogram to see the distribution of this proportion across our dataset. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
ggplot(df, aes(x = frac_black)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "#4C72B0", color = "white", boundary = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of residents who are Black, applicant's zip code",
    x = "Proportion Black",
    y = "Number of resumes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

## By converting an interval variables to an ordinal one
Imagine I wanted to say that the applicants are mostly from zipcodes with large proportions of Black people. We can see from the histogram that this isn't true. 

However, if I turn the interval variable `frac_black` into an *ordinal* one by creating skewed bins:

```{webr}
my_breaks <- c(seq(0, 0.2, by = 0.01), 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 1)
```

Then, the distribution of `frac_black` looks like something that fits my narrative more

```{webr}
df |>
  filter(!is.na(frac_black)) |>
  mutate(bin = cut(frac_black, breaks = my_breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bin)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#4C72B0", width = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of residents who are Black, applicant's zip code",
    x = "Proportion Black",
    y = "Number of resumes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_blank()
  )
```

## By selecting uninformative bin widths

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
ggplot(df, aes(x = frac_black)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "#4C72B0", color = "white", boundary = 0) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of residents who are Black, applicant's zip code",
    x = "Proportion Black",
    y = "Number of resumes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
